463.title: Where does the fire go?
463.hook: when a fire goes out, did it go north or south? the question doesn't fit
463.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers across traditions use the image of a flame going out to explain nirvana, and many temples light candles and lamps on altars as a reminder of the teaching.

segments.voice: Yesterday: step by step. Final knowledge comes by gradual training, from simply turning up to seeing for yourself. Which step did you take? Day four hundred sixty-three, a new week.

A birthday cake. Someone makes a wish and blows, and the little flames vanish, leaving thin gray ribbons of smoke. A five-year-old at the table asks: where did the fire go? Everyone laughs. But try answering. It didn't go to the kitchen. It didn't go up to the ceiling. The smoke did, but the smoke isn't the flame. A wanderer named Vacchagotta brings the Buddha a set of hard questions, the same ten from a few days ago, and the Buddha ends up asking him the five-year-old's question.
screen: `MAKE A WISH. BLOW.` → `WHERE DID THE FIRE GO?` → `VACCHAGOTTA'S QUESTIONS.`

segments.voice: Vacchagotta goes through the list. Is the world eternal? Is it not? Is the soul the same as the body? Does an awakened one exist after death? To each one, the Buddha says: I don't hold that view. Vacchagotta presses: do you have any view at all, then? The Buddha says he has put away views of that kind. What he has is seeing: how things arise and pass. Then Vacchagotta asks the hardest one: when a mind is fully freed, where does it reappear? Reappear doesn't apply, the Buddha says. Doesn't reappear? Doesn't apply. Both, neither? Doesn't apply. Vacchagotta is lost. I'm confused, he says. So the Buddha gives him the fire. If a fire were burning in front of you, would you know? Yes. And if someone asked what it was burning on? On grass and sticks. If it went out, would you know? Yes. Now, when it's out, which direction did it go: east, west, north or south? That doesn't apply, Vacchagotta says. It burned because of its fuel. When the fuel is used up and no more is added, it's simply counted as gone out. That's the answer. The question was built for things that travel. The word nibbāna, nirvana, draws on this very picture: going out, like a flame. The sutta doesn't say the freed one is annihilated, and it doesn't say they've gone somewhere else. It says they're deep and hard to measure, like the ocean. Buddhist schools have discussed this passage for centuries. The fire can't tell you north or south. The question doesn't fit.
screen: `I DON'T HOLD THAT VIEW.` · `REAPPEAR DOESN'T APPLY.` · `WHICH WAY DID THE FIRE GO?` · `DEEP, LIKE THE OCEAN.` · then, large: `THE QUESTION DOESN'T FIT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: blow out a candle and ask. If you have a candle or a match nearby, and it's safe, light it and watch the flame for a few breaths. If not, picture one. Notice how it depends on the wick and the wax. Then blow it out, or picture it going out. Watch the smoke. Ask quietly: where did it go? Don't answer. Just sit with how the question doesn't fit. The bell holds the time.
Where does the fire go? When a fire goes out, it didn't go north or south. It went out, because its fuel ran out. The Buddha's picture of nibbāna. Today's word.
screen: `WHERE DOES THE FIRE GO? — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the question doesn't fit. Today, when a question keeps going in circles, ask whether it's built for the thing you're asking about. Day four hundred sixty-three.

what a scholar hears: MN 72, the Aggivacchagotta Sutta; the fire simile and the image of the freed one as 'deep, immeasurable, hard to fathom like the ocean' are central texts in debates about nirvana.

464.title: Even that is a view
464.hook: a wanderer says "I accept no view"; Sariputta, fanning the Buddha, awakens
464.howItsDone: Buddhist traditions teach letting go of clinging to views, and the story of Sāriputta's awakening while fanning the Buddha is often told on retreats as a sign that insight can come in the middle of ordinary service.

segments.voice: Yesterday: where does the fire go? Not north or south. It went out. Your line was the question doesn't fit. Did you catch a question built for the wrong thing? Day four hundred sixty-four.

A dinner table, and everyone is arguing about something. One guest leans back and says: I don't have opinions. I'm above all that. It sounds wise. It sounds humble, even. On Vulture Peak, outside the city of Rājagaha, in a cave called the Boar's Cave, a wanderer named Dīghanakha, Long-Nails, comes to the Buddha and says almost exactly that. Standing behind the Buddha, fanning him, is Sāriputta. Tradition says he has been a monk for about two weeks. He is only there to keep the air moving.
screen: `I DON'T HAVE OPINIONS.` → `THE BOAR'S CAVE, VULTURE PEAK.` → `SĀRIPUTTA, FANNING.`

segments.voice: Dīghanakha's words, in paraphrase: nothing is acceptable to me. No view at all. The Buddha's reply is gentle and almost funny. This view of yours, that nothing is acceptable to you: is that view acceptable to you? Long-Nails sees the trap at once, and tries to wriggle. Even if it were, it would be the same. But the point has landed. Saying I hold no views is itself a view, and one that can hide behind looking neutral. The Buddha doesn't win the argument and leave. He describes how views of every kind, everything is acceptable, nothing is, some things are, lead to clinging and quarrel, and how a wise person, seeing that, lets go of the clinging. Then he turns to the body and to feeling. When you feel a pleasant feeling, you're not feeling a painful one at that moment. Each feeling comes and goes; none of them is worth grasping as me or mine. Then comes the turn. The sutta says that while Sāriputta stood there fanning, he reflected on what he heard, and his mind was freed from clinging. The commentary says Dīghanakha was his nephew. One man came to argue and left with a first glimpse of the teaching. The other was just doing a service, moving the air, and woke up. The practice wasn't a better opinion. It was noticing the grip that any opinion, even the opinion of having none, can have on us.
screen: `NOTHING IS ACCEPTABLE TO ME.` · `IS THAT VIEW ACCEPTABLE TO YOU?` · `VIEWS LEAD TO CLINGING.` · `SĀRIPUTTA, FANNING, IS FREED.` · then, large: `EVEN THAT IS A VIEW.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice one view about views. Sit and settle. Let one strong opinion come to mind, about politics, about family, about how people should behave. Notice how tightly it's held. Then look for an opinion behind the opinion, if there is one: maybe that you're the reasonable one, or above it all. Just notice it. Don't drop it, don't defend it. See whether the grip changes on the out-breath. The bell holds the time.
Even that is a view. A wanderer claimed to hold no views, and the Buddha asked if he held that one. Sāriputta, listening, was freed. Today's word.
screen: `EVEN THAT IS A VIEW — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: even that is a view. Today, when you catch yourself above an argument, ask: is that view acceptable to me? Day four hundred sixty-four.

465.title: The leper by the fire
465.hook: a man with leprosy scratches his sores by the fire and calls it pleasure
465.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers use this simile to explain why monastics and serious lay practitioners restrain the senses: not because pleasure is evil, but because craving feeds itself, and a calm mind finds deeper ease.

segments.voice: Yesterday: even that is a view, and Sāriputta, fanning the Buddha, set free. Did you notice the opinion behind one of your opinions? Day four hundred sixty-five.

A mosquito bite on the ankle. Scratching it is a bad idea, and it gets scratched anyway, and for a few seconds that feels like relief. Then it's worse. A wandering ascetic named Māgandiya hears that the Buddha teaches restraint of the senses, and he's offended. He calls the Buddha a destroyer of growth, someone who kills off life's pleasures. The Buddha doesn't get defensive. He tells Māgandiya about his own youth: three palaces, one for each season, musicians, pleasures on offer. He gave it all up. Why would anyone do that? He answers with a picture far stronger than a mosquito bite.
screen: `THE MOSQUITO BITE.` → `A DESTROYER OF GROWTH?` → `THREE PALACES, GIVEN UP.`

segments.voice: Suppose, the Buddha says, there were a man with leprosy, his body covered in sores. His only relief is to scratch the sores with his nails and to hold his body close over a pit of burning coals. The heat eases the itch. To him, it feels good. Now suppose a physician comes and cures him. He's healthy, free, able to go where he likes. Would he envy another sick man scratching by the fire? No. Would he want to go back? No. And if two strong men tried to drag him toward the coals, he'd twist and fight to get away. The fire hasn't changed. The coals are as hot as ever. What changed is his health. When he was sick, his senses were damaged, and so he took something painful to be pleasant. That's the Buddha's point about cravings, and it isn't puritan. He doesn't say pleasure is evil. He says some of what we call pleasure is relief from an itch the craving itself keeps making. The more you scratch, the more it itches. Then the Buddha speaks a verse: health is the greatest gain, nibbāna the highest happiness. Māgandiya says he has heard those very words from his own teachers. So what is this health? Māgandiya rubs his own arms and legs: this is health. The Buddha says he knows the words, but not yet what they point to. A similar verse appears in the Dhammapada, in Max Müller's words: "Health is the greatest of gifts, contentedness the best riches; trust is the best of relationships, Nirvâna the highest happiness." The healed man doesn't hate the fire. He just doesn't need it anymore.
screen: `SORES, AND A PIT OF COALS.` · `THE PHYSICIAN CURES HIM.` · `THE FIRE IS THE SAME. HE ISN'T.` · `HEALTH, THE GREATEST GIFT.` · then, large: `THE LEPER'S FIRE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: spot one scratching habit. Sit and settle. Think of one thing you reach for that brings relief more than joy: checking, snacking, refreshing, re-reading an old argument. Picture the moment just before you reach. Feel the itch there, the restlessness. Breathe into it without scratching. Notice that it rises and, if you wait, begins to fade. Stay with the breath. The bell holds the time.
The leper by the fire. A sick man finds relief in burning coals and calls it pleasure; once healed, he wouldn't go near them. Today's word.
screen: `THE LEPER BY THE FIRE — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the leper's fire. Today, when you reach for a scratch, pause once and ask: is this joy, or relief from an itch? Day four hundred sixty-five.

466.title: Tested teachings
466.hook: four ways that undo the holy life and four that give no comfort
466.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers in several traditions encourage students to test teachings in their own experience rather than accept them on authority alone, sometimes citing this sutta alongside the Kālāma Sutta.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the leper by the fire, who called relief pleasure until he was healed. Your line was the leper's fire. Did you pause before one scratch? Day four hundred sixty-six.

Evening, by a pool near the city of Kosambī. A wanderer named Sandaka is sitting with a big group of his students, and they're loud, talking about kings and armies and food and gossip, the way any group talks. Then he sees Ānanda walking toward them and hushes everyone. Quiet, he says. Here comes one of the Buddha's monks. They like quiet. Sandaka invites him to say something about his teacher's way. And Ānanda, rather than praising it, starts with how to tell when a way of life isn't worth following.
screen: `A LOUD EVENING BY A POOL.` → `QUIET, HERE COMES A MONK.` → `HOW TO TELL.`

segments.voice: Ānanda describes eight cases. Four, he says, undo the holy life completely. They're teachings that say, in different ways, that what you do makes no difference: no fruit from good or bad action, no cause for purity, everything fixed in advance. If that's the teaching, a sensible person reasons: then why train at all? The text names views held by some teachers of that time; this lesson keeps to the shape of the argument. The next four are more interesting, because they're not wrong exactly. They just give no comfort. First, a teacher who claims to know and see everything, always. Yet he walks into an empty house and gets no food, gets bitten by a dog, meets a wild elephant, and has to ask people's names and the way to the village. Second, a teacher who relies only on tradition, what has been handed down. Some of it is well remembered and some isn't; some is true, some isn't. Third, a teacher who relies only on reasoning. Some of it is well reasoned, some badly; it could go either way. Fourth, a teacher who is simply confused, and when asked a question wriggles like an eel. In each case, Ānanda says, a wise person notices, and quietly looks elsewhere. And he doesn't say, trust us instead. He goes on to describe a training a person can check for themselves: conduct, then calm, then understanding, each with results that can be seen. The same caution shows up elsewhere in the Pali texts: a teaching isn't settled by authority, tradition or cleverness alone. Look at what it does in a life.
screen: `FOUR WAYS THAT UNDO THE TRAINING.` · `THE ALL-KNOWING TEACHER, BITTEN BY A DOG.` · `TRADITION ALONE. REASON ALONE.` · `THE EEL-WRIGGLER.` · then, large: `TEST THE TEACHING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hold one teaching to the test. Sit and settle. Choose one idea you've been living by, from a book, a parent, a podcast, even from this path. Ask three things, slowly. Do I hold it only because it was handed to me? Only because it sounds clever? What has it actually done in my life, and in the lives of people who follow it? Let the answers be honest. Then rest with the breath. The bell holds the time.
Tested teachings. Ānanda's eight cases: four teachings that undo the holy life, and four that give no comfort, from claimed omniscience to eel-wriggling. Today's word.
Your line: test the teaching. Today, when you hear a confident claim, ask what it does in a life, not only who said it. Day four hundred sixty-six.

original.note: Pali anussava: what is heard and handed down, oral tradition. one of the four uncertain grounds.

trapdoor: what you thought: tested teachings means teachings that passed an exam.
what it means: ways of life you can check by their results, not by claims, tradition or cleverness alone.

467.title: Ratthapala's fast
467.hook: a young man fasts until his parents let him ordain; years later they try to tempt him home
467.howItsDone: In Theravada practice a candidate for ordination is asked whether their parents consent, and monks may return to visit family; in some countries young men ordain for a short time partly to honor their parents.

segments.voice: Yesterday: tested teachings, and Ānanda's eight cases. Your line was test the teaching. Did you ask what one confident claim actually does in a life? Day four hundred sixty-seven.

Raṭṭhapāla is the only son of a wealthy family in a town in the Kuru country. He hears the Buddha teach once, and he knows. He wants to go forth, to become a monk. The Buddha says he can't ordain anyone without their parents' consent. So Raṭṭhapāla goes home and asks. They say no. He's their only child, dear to them, raised in comfort. He asks again. No. So he lies down on the bare floor and says: I will either die right here, or go forth.
screen: `AN ONLY SON.` → `NOT WITHOUT YOUR PARENTS' CONSENT.` → `HE LIES DOWN ON THE BARE FLOOR.`

segments.voice: He doesn't eat. One meal, two, three, up to seven, the sutta says. His parents beg. His friends come and beg. Get up, eat, enjoy your life, you can do good as a householder. He says nothing. Finally the friends go to the parents: if you refuse, he'll die. If you let him go, at least you'll see him alive. And they agree, on one condition: after he's ordained, he must come back to visit. Later, he does, as a monk, walking for alms in his own hometown. His father is in the hall having his hair dressed, sees a shaven-headed monk at the door, and doesn't recognize his own son. He mutters against the monks who took his only child, and Raṭṭhapāla gets nothing, not even a polite refusal. On his way out, a family servant is about to throw away yesterday's porridge. He asks her to put it in his bowl. And as she does, she knows him, by his hands, his feet, his voice. She runs to his mother. The next day his father piles up gold and silver in the house. Take this, he says. Come home. Enjoy your wealth and do good. Raṭṭhapāla's former wives are dressed in their finest. He answers his father calmly: put it all on carts, and sink it in the Ganges. It will only bring you grief. He stood by it. Not by shouting, or by cutting his family off, but by coming back exactly as he'd promised, eating their old porridge, and saying no kindly. The fast was the drama. The visit was the proof.
screen: `SEVEN MEALS WITHOUT EATING.` · `YOU MUST COME BACK TO VISIT.` · `THE SERVANT KNOWS HIS HANDS.` · `GOLD, AND A CALM NO.` · then, large: `HE STOOD BY IT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: stand by one choice kindly. Sit and settle. Think of one choice you've made that someone you love doesn't like, a job, a move, a belief, a way of living. Picture their face. Notice any urge to defend yourself loudly, or to give in. Then picture a third way: staying with your choice and staying warm toward them, the way Raṭṭhapāla came home and ate the porridge. Breathe with that. The bell holds the time.
Raṭṭhapāla's fast. An only son lies on the floor until his parents let him go forth, and later comes home as he promised, and kindly says no to their gold. Today's word.
Your line: he stood by it. Today, hold one choice steady with someone who disagrees, and be kind while you do. Day four hundred sixty-seven.

468.title: Four summaries
468.hook: the world is swept away, has no protector, owns nothing, is a slave to craving
468.howItsDone: Buddhist monastics and lay practitioners reflect regularly on impermanence and the limits of possessions, and teachers use Raṭṭhapāla's four summaries as a short framework for that reflection.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Raṭṭhapāla's fast, the only son who lay on the floor until he could go forth. Your line was he stood by it. Did you hold one choice kindly? Day four hundred sixty-eight.

Same sutta, second half. Raṭṭhapāla has left his family's house and is sitting under a tree in the king's park. King Koravya comes out for a stroll, recognizes him, and sits down with real curiosity. People go forth, the king says, for four reasons: they're old, or sick, or they've lost their money, or they've lost their family. You're young. You're healthy. Your family is rich and alive. So why? It's a fair question. The kind a friend asks over coffee when you've quit a good job.
screen: `UNDER A TREE IN THE KING'S PARK.` → `OLD, SICK, BROKE, OR BEREAVED?` → `NONE OF THEM. SO WHY?`

segments.voice: Raṭṭhapāla answers with four short sayings he heard from the Buddha. He calls them summaries of the teaching. One: the world is swept away; it does not last. Two: the world has no shelter, no one in charge to protect it. Three: the world owns nothing; you have to leave everything and go on. Four: the world is never full, never satisfied, a slave to craving. Then, instead of leaving them abstract, he asks the king four questions, one for each. When you were twenty-five, how were you at riding, at archery, with a sword? Strong, says the king. Sometimes I thought I had no equal. And now? Now I'm eighty. Sometimes I mean to step one way and my foot goes another. That's the first: swept away. Do you have an illness? Wind trouble, says the king. When it comes, can your ministers and relatives take some of the pain for you? No. I have to feel it all alone. That's the second: no shelter. These treasures you have now, will you take them with you? No. Third: you own nothing. And last: if a trusted man came from the east and said there's a rich country there you could conquer, would you? Yes. And beyond the ocean? Yes, that too. Fourth: never full. Raṭṭhapāla doesn't preach at the king. He lets the king's own life answer. The four summaries aren't meant to make the world look grim. In this sutta they're the reason a young man with everything chose a simpler life, and they're true of kings too.
screen: `SWEPT AWAY: AT TWENTY-FIVE, AND AT EIGHTY.` · `NO SHELTER: NOBODY FEELS YOUR PAIN.` · `OWNS NOTHING: YOU LEAVE IT ALL.` · `NEVER FULL: AND BEYOND THE OCEAN?` · then, large: `THE WORLD IS SWEPT AWAY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: reflect on one of the four. Sit and settle. Choose one: swept away, no shelter, owns nothing, or never full. Let it touch something real in your life: how your body has changed in ten years, a pain only you could feel, a thing you'll leave behind, a want that keeps moving. Don't push for a feeling. Just let the summary be true for a few breaths, and notice what softens. The bell holds the time.
Four summaries. The world is swept away, has no shelter, owns nothing, and is never full. Raṭṭhapāla's answer to a king who asked why he left. Today's word.
Your line: the world is swept away. Today, notice one thing changing that you'd assumed would stay the same, and let it be swept, gently. Day four hundred sixty-eight.

original.note: Pali: 'the world is swept away; it does not last.' the first of the four summaries.

trapdoor: what you thought: the world is swept away sounds like a disaster.
what it means: nothing in life stands still: strength, health, possessions and wants all move.

469.title: The first gray hair
469.hook: King Makhadeva tells his barber to report the first gray hair, and then goes forth
469.howItsDone: Buddhists in several countries take temporary or late-life ordination, and older lay people often deepen their practice, keeping extra precepts and spending more time at the temple, as a way of answering the 'messengers' of age.

segments.voice: Yesterday: four summaries. Swept away, no shelter, owns nothing, never full. Your line was the world is swept away. What did you notice changing? Day four hundred sixty-nine, the end of a week.

The bathroom mirror, a Tuesday morning, and there it is: one gray hair, wiry, catching the light. It can be plucked, dyed, or laughed off. Or it can be read as news. The Buddha is walking through a mango grove near the city of Mithilā, and at one spot he smiles. Ānanda knows the Buddha doesn't smile without a reason, and asks why. The Buddha tells him a story about a king who once lived on this very ground, and his barber, and a pair of tweezers.
screen: `ONE GRAY HAIR IN THE MIRROR.` → `THE BUDDHA SMILES.` → `A KING, A BARBER, TWEEZERS.`

segments.voice: Long ago, the story goes, a good king named Makhādeva ruled here. And he gave his barber an unusual order: whenever you see gray hairs growing on my head, tell me. Years pass, many years in the story's long, legendary count. One day the barber sees one. He plucks it out with tweezers and lays it in the king's palm. The king looks at it and says the gray hairs are messengers of the gods, and they've arrived. It's time. He gives the barber a whole village as thanks. He calls his eldest son and hands him the kingdom. And he asks one thing: when you see your first gray hair, do the same. Pass the kingdom on, and go forth. Then he shaves his head, puts on robes, and lives the rest of his life in this same mango grove, filling the world around him with kindness and compassion. His son keeps the promise, and his son's son, for a long line of kings. Until one king doesn't. The good custom ends with him. Then the Buddha reveals two things. First, I was King Makhādeva. Second, that old practice was good, but it led only to a heavenly world. What I teach now, he says, leads all the way to peace and awakening. And he gives Ānanda the same charge the old king gave his son: keep this good practice going. Don't be the last one. The gray hair isn't a tragedy in this story. It's a messenger. Its message isn't, you're old. It's, the time you were waiting for has come.
screen: `TELL ME WHEN YOU SEE GRAY.` · `MESSENGERS OF THE GODS.` · `PASS IT ON, AND GO FORTH.` · `DON'T BE THE LAST ONE.` · then, large: `THE FIRST GRAY HAIR.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look for your gray hair. Sit and settle. Ask yourself: what is my messenger? It may not be a hair. A slower knee, a child who no longer needs you, a friend's diagnosis, a birthday with a zero. Let one come to mind. Instead of flinching, ask what it might be inviting you to begin, or to pass on. Breathe with that question. The bell holds the time.
The first gray hair. King Makhādeva's barber laid it in his palm, and the king called it a messenger and went forth. Today's word.

Your line: the first gray hair. Treat one sign of time today as a messenger, not an enemy. And that's week sixty-seven: the fire, even that is a view, the leper's fire, tested teachings, Raṭṭhapāla's fast, four summaries, and the first gray hair. Day four hundred sixty-nine.
screen: `WEEK SIXTY-SEVEN: FIRE · VIEWS · THE LEPER'S FIRE · TESTED · RATTHAPALA · FOUR SUMMARIES · GRAY HAIR`

fork.setup: you're King Makhādeva. your barber has just laid a gray hair in your palm. what do you do?
options: hand the kingdom to your son and go forth
fork.reveal: he calls the gray hairs messengers of the gods, gives the barber a village, passes the kingdom on and goes forth.

original.note: Pali devadūta: messenger of the gods. the name the king gives his gray hairs.

trapdoor: what you thought: a gray hair means you're getting old.
what it means: in this story, a messenger: the time you were waiting for has come.

what a scholar hears: MN 83, the Makhādeva Sutta; the same story appears in the Jātakas, and 'messengers of the gods' (devadūta) echoes the old man, sick man and corpse of the Buddha's own life story.
